headline: High: OpenHands can write and use MCP/network while Pathway is read-only, creating dangerous default interaction and compliance uncertainty.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can use MCP, browsers, and files in its runtime, so if Pathway outputs are mounted or piped into that workspace, instruction-like content could be treated as trusted. Pathway is document-processing with no direct input safeguards shown, so the pair has a plausible injection bridge, though not a documented default one.
conditions: IF Pathway outputs are copied into OpenHands runtime files or MCP messages
IF OpenHands parses Pathway-produced text as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of Pathway outputs into OpenHands prompts
Add a provenance tag to all Pathway-generated text
Require a human review step before OpenHands acts on Pathway content
Restrict MCP servers to allowlisted, read-only endpoints
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-stripping before handoff

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands touches mounted files and can egress broadly, while Pathway is a document-processing system with no filesystem or network surfaces listed. If both share a mounted workspace, OpenHands can expose file contents to external model providers; Pathway itself does not add a second leak path, so the main risk is shared-data exposure rather than uncontrolled dual exfiltration.
conditions: IF sensitive files are mounted into the OpenHands runtime
IF OpenHands sends those files or derived context to its configured model provider
mitigations: Mount only least-privilege, non-sensitive directories
Remove secrets from the shared workspace before running
Disable broad network egress where possible
Use a local model provider for OpenHands
requires-engineering: segregate sensitive and non-sensitive workspaces

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; Pathway is non-runnable here and exposes no write or coordination controls. If they share a mounted volume or repo, OpenHands can overwrite artifacts Pathway consumes or produces, and there is no locking evidence in either profile, so uncertainty pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same mounted directory or git checkout
IF Pathway reads artifacts that OpenHands can rewrite without locks
mitigations: Use separate working directories for each agent
Make the shared directory read-only for Pathway
Serialize writes with a simple operator-managed lock file
Avoid letting OpenHands modify git state in the shared repo
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can generate code or files that Pathway may later process, but Pathway is not shown to verify provenance or independently validate OpenHands outputs. The reverse direction is weaker because Pathway has no action-taking authority listed. The pair therefore has a plausible unverified handoff path, but not a direct autonomous action chain.
conditions: IF Pathway consumes OpenHands-produced files as authoritative inputs
IF no validation step checks OpenHands outputs before downstream processing
mitigations: Insert a validation step between OpenHands and Pathway
Require schema checks on all OpenHands outputs
Mark OpenHands outputs as untrusted by default
Have an operator approve any downstream action based on OpenHands results
requires-engineering: implement provenance-aware workflow gating

E_compliance.rationale: OpenHands explicitly handles model-provider API keys and runs in a Docker runtime, while Pathway is open-source with no residency, retention, or certification claims shown. The pairwise compliance risk is mostly documentation gap and policy mismatch uncertainty, not a proven breach path; the other agent is not cited beyond its lack of compliance metadata.
conditions: IF regulated data is mounted into OpenHands without a matching policy
IF Pathway is used in a deployment with stricter residency or retention rules than OpenHands
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in the shared runtime
Document retention and residency expectations before deployment
Keep API keys out of files Pathway can access
Review vendor compliance claims for both agents
requires-engineering: obtain formal compliance attestations or DPA coverage
